newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany has no idea of NATO expansion cost - deputy.
newsitem.headline: Germany has no idea of NATO expansion cost - deputy.

text.p: Germany's cash-strapped government has no idea how much NATO's planned enlargement into Eastern Europe will cost and should produce a full financial projection for parliament soon, a deputy said on Tuesday.

Juergen Koppelin, a Free Democrat (FDP) deputy responsible for defence issues in parliament's budget committee, said the government had told him in reply to questions that it could not say how much Bonn would have to pay for the programme.

NATO and Russia signed a treaty in Paris on Tuesday for a new security partnership that clears the way for the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) to invite new members to join the alliance at a special summit in Madrid in July.

Koppelin's statement showed how Bonn's budgetary problems as it strains to meet the criteria for Europe's monetary union (EMU) have started to raise questions about a wide array of government spending plans, even for programmes like NATO expansion which Chancellor Helmut Kohl strongly supports.
"While NATO expansion is very welcome politically, one must ask which financial burdens it will impose on current NATO states," Koppelin said in a statement.

Citing United States estimates that Bonn may have to pay a billion marks ($590 million) annually for the next 10 years to help new members meet NATO technical standards, he said it was "astonishing that the government supposedly has no projection of the costs of this coming financial burden."
Koppelin said he would ask in his capacity as defence rapporteur for the budget committee for a full financial report from the government on NATO expansion.

Koppelin has raised the cost issue in the past, only to see officials like Defence Minister Volker Ruehe play down the financial aspect and highlight the added security Germany would gain by having former enemies turned into NATO alliles.
Ruehe told RTL television on May 14 that opponents of NATO expansion were using the cost argument to delay the plan.

Some defence industry interests were spreading the word that new members had to buy new western aircraft or tanks in order to cash in on the move, he said. "We have a lot of old tanks in NATO now, that was never a condition," he said.

"The issue is not financing the modernisation these countries are conducting anyway -- they have to do that themselves," he said. "We can take time building up common infrastructures ... so we're talking about modest sums."

In its written reply to Koppelin's original questions, the government said: "The federal government has not yet made its own cost estimates because it appeared too early in view of the many uncertainties involved."

It could also not answer a specific question about how much it would cost Bonn over the next 10 years if Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- the most likely candidates for the first round of expansion -- joined the Atlantic Alliance.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said in April that expansion would cost new members up to one billion dollars annually. Existing members would pay an extra $600-$800 million per year for regional reinforcement while direct expansion-related costs were about $900 million a year.
